claim: The auditory cortex (AC) sends extensive feedback to the inferior colliculus (IC).
source: Auditory cortex sends extensive projections to IC (Bajo and Moore, 2005; Bajo et al., 2007; Coomes et al., 2005; Doucet et al., 2003; Saldaña et al., 1996; Winer et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Activation of cortico-collicular feedback increased spontaneous activity in IC.
source: Activation of feedback increased spontaneous activity and decreased stimulus selectivity in IC, whereas suppression had no effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Activation of cortico-collicular feedback decreased stimulus selectivity in IC.
source: Activation of feedback increased spontaneous activity and decreased stimulus selectivity in IC, whereas suppression had no effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Suppression of cortico-collicular feedback had no effect on IC activity.
source: Activation of feedback increased spontaneous activity and decreased stimulus selectivity in IC, whereas suppression had no effect.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Modulating the activity of parvalbumin-positive (PV) inhibitory interneurons did not affect IC sound-evoked activity.
source: We found that modulating the activity of either type of interneuron did not affect IC sound-evoked activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Modulating the activity of somatostatin-positive (SST) inhibitory interneurons did not affect IC sound-evoked activity.
source: We found that modulating the activity of either type of interneuron did not affect IC sound-evoked activity.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Activation of excitatory projections affects collicular sound responses.
source: Combined, our results identify that activation of excitatory projections, but not inhibition-driven changes in cortical activity, affects collicular sound responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Inhibition-driven changes in cortical activity do not affect collicular sound responses.
source: Combined, our results identify that activation of excitatory projections, but not inhibition-driven changes in cortical activity, affects collicular sound responses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Cortico-collicular feedback is critical to auditory learning, specifically learning to adapt to a unilateral earplug during sound localization.
source: Cortico-collicular feedback is critical to auditory learning, specifically learning to adapt to a unilateral earplug during sound localization (Bajo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Cortico-collicular feedback was necessary to induce running in response to a loud noise.
source: Furthermore, cortico-collicular feedback was necessary to induce running in response to a loud noise (Xiong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: IC receives glutamatergic inputs from neurons originating predominantly in layer 5 of AC.
source: IC receives glutamatergic (Feliciano and Potashner, 1995) inputs from neurons originating predominantly in layer 5 of AC (Bajo and Moore, 2005; Bajo et al., 2007; Coomes et al., 2005; Doucet et al., 2003; Saldaña et al., 1996; Winer et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Activation of cortico-collicular neurons resulted in an increase in firing rate of IC neurons at 1 ms laser duration (p=5.3e-4, ON = 5.6 ± 0.6 Hz, OFF = 4.9 ± 0.5 Hz).
source: This effect persisted at the 5 ms, 25 ms, and 250 ms laser duration (Figure 2C; 1 ms: p=5.3e-4, ON = 5.6 ± 0.6 Hz, OFF = 4.9 ± 0.5 Hz; 5 ms: p=0.0027, ON = 6.9 ± 0.7 Hz, OFF = 4.8 ± 0.5 Hz; 250 ms: p=0.005, ON = 5.6 ± 0.6 Hz, OFF = 4.8 ± 0.5 Hz).
evidence: Supported by experimental data with statistical analysis

claim: Suppressing cortico-collicular feedback using ArchT had little difference in firing in IC neurons at 25 ms laser duration (p=0.039, ON = 9.5 ± 0.7 Hz, OFF = 9.5 ± 0.7 Hz).

claim: SST suppression resulted in an increase in spontaneous, but not tone-evoked activity in IC.
source: Whereas modulating PVs did not have an effect on IC activity, SST suppression resulted in an increase in spontaneous, but not tone-evoked activity in IC, which suggests that inhibitory modulation of sound responses in AC does not propagate to IC.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: Inhibitory modulation of sound responses in AC does not propagate to IC.
source: Whereas modulating PVs did not have an effect on IC activity, SST suppression resulted in an increase in spontaneous, but not tone-evoked activity in IC, which suggests that inhibitory modulation of sound responses in AC does not propagate to IC.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that inhibitory interneuron modulation affects AC but not IC sound responses

claim: Direct cortico-collicular feedback can modulate responses to simple (pure tones) and more complex (DRCs) auditory stimuli by reducing, rather than increasing, sound selectivity.
source: Overall our findings imply that direct cortico-collicular feedback can modulate responses to simple (pure tones) and more complex (DRCs) auditory stimuli by reducing, rather than increasing, sound selectivity.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of tone and DRC experiments

claim: Cortico-collicular modulation occurs independently of the activity of cortical inhibitory interneurons.
source: This modulation occurs independently of the activity of cortical inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of effect of inhibitory interneuron modulation on IC sound responses

claim: Cortical stimulation shifted tuning properties of IC neurons toward those of the stimulated neurons in frequency.
source: Previous studies found that electrical stimulation of AC caused best frequencies in IC to shift towards the best frequencies of the stimulated site in AC (Gao and Suga, 1998; Gao and Suga, 2000; Ma and Suga, 2001a; Yan et al., 2005; Yan and Suga, 1998; Zhou and Jen, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Cortico-collicular feedback may be important for increasing the representation of behaviorally relevant stimuli in IC.
source: These results suggest that cortico-collicular feedback may be important for increasing the representation of behaviorally relevant stimuli in IC.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on prior literature findings

claim: When activating direct feedback, we did not observe consistent changes in best frequency of IC neurons.
source: However, when activating direct feedback, we did not observe consistent changes in best frequency of IC neurons (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in Figure 6D

claim: The lack of consistent changes in best frequency may be due to activation of feedback projections across cortex, and therefore across the tonotopic map.
source: This may be due to activation of feedback projections across cortex, and therefore across the tonotopic map, in this paradigm.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed lack of best frequency changes

claim: Previous studies found no effect of activating projection terminals on responses in the CNIC, only shell regions of IC.
source: Previous studies found no effect of activating projection terminals on responses in the CNIC, only shell regions of IC (Xiong et al., 2015), which are the predominant targets of cortico-collicular feedback.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: The effects in central IC may be due to direct cortico-collicular feedback, intra-collicular circuits, or a combination of these mechanisms.
source: The effects in central IC may be due to direct cortico-collicular feedback, intra-collicular circuits (Malmierca et al., 1995; Miller et al., 2005; Saldaña and Merchań, 1992; Sturm et al., 2014), or a combination of these mechanisms.
evidence: Speculative interpretation with citations to prior literature on intra-collicular circuits

claim: Previous inactivation studies have shown mixed effects on sound-evoked responses in IC, but consistently demonstrated no effect on frequency selectivity.
source: Previous inactivation studies have shown mixed effects on sound-evoked responses in IC, but consistently demonstrated no effect on frequency selectivity, agreeing with our results.
evidence: Supported by comparison with prior literature

claim: At baseline the cortex provides only weak modulation of IC activity.
source: Combined, these studies suggest that at baseline the cortex provides only weak modulation of IC activity.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of current results with prior inactivation studies

claim: The IC is a critical structure in the PPI circuit.
source: The IC is a critical structure in the PPI circuit (Fendt et al., 2001; Leitner and Cohen, 1985; Li et al., 1998), with the central nucleus of IC receiving ascending auditory projections and the external nucleus of IC acting as the output station (Fendt et al., 2001; Li and Yue, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Cortico-collicular neurons send collaterals not only to IC, but also to the auditory thalamus, amygdala, and striatum.
source: An important consideration with this method, however, is that these neurons do not only send collaterals to IC, but also to the auditory thalamus (Asokan et al., 2018; Williamson and Polley, 2019), amygdala (Asokan et al., 2018), and striatum (Asokan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: There is evidence of descending projections to IC from thalamus and amygdala.
source: There is also evidence of descending projections to IC from thalamus (Winer et al., 2002) and amygdala (Marsh et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The effects observed from activating cortico-collicular feedback may be due, at least in part, to secondary pathways through thalamus and amygdala.
source: When interpreting our results, it is important to consider that the effects we observe from activating cortico-collicular feedback may also be due, at least in part, to these secondary pathways.
evidence: Speculative consideration of alternative explanations for observed effects

claim: A more complex stimulation pattern potentially can achieve stronger activation than a square pulse.
source: One caveat is that we used a square pulse for optogenetic manipulations, whereas a more complex stimulation pattern potentially can achieve stronger activation (Vila et al., 2019).
evidence: Speculative consideration with citation to prior literature

claim: The lack of effect observed with suppression of cortico-collicular feedback may be due to the lack of task engagement.
source: It is possible that the lack of effect we observe with suppression of cortico-collicular feedback is due to the lack of task engagement.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed results

claim: Task engagement modulates neuronal responses to sounds.
source: Furthermore, studies have found that task engagement modulates neuronal responses to sounds (Downer et al., 2017; Fritz et al., 2003; Kuchibhotla et al., 2017; Lakatos et al., 2013; McGinley et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Suppression of the cortico-collicular pathway would be expected to affect sound processing in IC during a behavioral task.
source: Thus, we would expect suppression of this pathway to affect sound processing in IC during a behavioral task.
evidence: Speculative prediction based on prior literature and current results
